name: Caribbean Green
lede: Caribbean Green is a bright, saturated teal that Wikipedia lists among Crayola's colors, and a color our painting archive never once finds, a sign of just how far this hue sits from anything the old pigments could make.

sections.title: A place name, a web-only source
sections.body:
Our only sources for this color are Wikipedia, which credits it to Crayola, and the classification here tagging "Caribbean" as a place word [1]. Neither explains when or why the name was chosen, and no book consulted here documents it at all [1]. The ISCC-NBS system would place it as a brilliant green, a close fit at only 2.1 units from that block's center, and the Munsell notation is 6.7G 7.2/10.1 [1].

The closest named color on screen is [[imperial-green]], 4.5 units away and read as darker than Caribbean Green; [[mountain-meadow]] follows at 4.8, duller and darker still, [[medium-aquamarine]] at 5.7, duller, and [[green-crayola]] at 6.9, darker [3]. In printed sources the term itself first appears around 1940, rises through the 1980s and peaks around 2000, a timeline that fits a mid-to-late-20th-century color name more than an old one [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our 23,781-painting archive has this color covering at least 1 percent of its canvas, within a color difference of 4, as photographed [2]. That describes this archive, which leans toward historical and varnished paintings, rather than painting as a whole; a saturated, cool, screen-bright teal like this one is simply not a color old oil and tempera pigments reproduce easily [2]. It is the kind of honest gap that shows the limits of matching screen colors against centuries of aged canvas, rather than a claim that no painter ever used anything like it [2].

openers: Caribbean Green never once appears, at any real size, across 23,781 paintings in our archive.
In print, the term "Caribbean Green" barely existed before 1940 and only took off after 1980.

issues: Only a web source (Wikipedia/Crayola); no book in our library documents this name.
Zero archive presence reflects this archive's historical-painting bias, not painting in general.
